Small glands that help your immune syste: Small glands that help your immune system filter lymph fluid. Some are in the armpit and near the breast.
Fat surrounds the glands and ducts and c: Fat surrounds the glands and ducts and contributes to the breast’s shape and size. The amount varies from person to person.
Small groups of glands that can make mil: Small groups of glands that can make milk during breastfeeding.
Small tubes that carry milk from the lob: Small tubes that carry milk from the lobules towards the nipple.
The area of darker skin around the nippl: The area of darker skin around the nipple. Small glands here help keep the skin protected.
The area at the centre of the areola whe: The area at the centre of the areola where milk can leave through small openings. Nipples naturally vary in appearance.
A new lump or an area that feels thicker: A new lump or an area that feels thicker than usual can have different causes. Have a new or unusual change checked, even if it does not hurt.
Notice new puckering, dimpling, redness: Notice new puckering, dimpling, redness or changes in skin texture. These can have different causes and should be discussed with a healthcare professional.
A nipple that newly turns inward, a pers: A nipple that newly turns inward, a persistent rash, or unexpected discharge deserves assessment. Discharge that happens without squeezing, especially if bloody, should be checked.

Breasts can change with hormones, age an: Breasts can change with hormones, age and other factors. A new or unusual change in shape or size, especially on one side, should be assessed.
Screening looks for signs of breast canc: Screening looks for signs of breast cancer before symptoms appear, often using a mammogram (an X-ray of the breast). When and how often screening is offered depends on local guidance, age and individual circumstances. Ask a healthcare professional what is appropriate for you. A new breast change needs assessment rather than waiting for routine screening.
Seeking advice about a breast change.
A healthcare professional may ask about: A healthcare professional may ask about the change and your health history, then examine your breasts and nearby areas. They should explain what they are doing, and you can ask questions. They may suggest further tests or a referral to understand the change.
Depending on the assessment, next steps: Depending on the assessment, next steps may include an ultrasound, a mammogram or a biopsy (a small tissue sample). Not everyone needs every test. Results help guide a discussion about what, if any, further care is needed. Ask how and when you will receive results, and what follow-up is recommended.
